analysis.one_liner: Opens protected federal lands and waters to oil drilling and fast-tracks refinery permits.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This 2008 bill, written when gas was over $4 a gallon, would have wiped out every federal prohibition on leasing federal lands and offshore waters for oil, gas, and oil shale drilling. When crude oil traded at $100 a barrel or more, the Interior Secretary would have been required to waive federal drilling permit requirements altogether. It also would have made the Department of Energy the boss of all refinery permits, with the power to automatically approve any project an agency failed to clear within 30 days.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain access to protected public lands, offshore waters, and oil shale deposits without the leasing bans that had kept them off-limits, and would be able to drill without federal drilling permits whenever oil topped $100 a barrel. Companies seeking to build refineries would face a faster, centralized permitting process.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that any federal law prohibiting leasing of federal lands or submerged lands for oil, gas, or oil shale exploration and production 'shall have no force or effect,' ending the offshore drilling moratorium that covered over 80% of the Outer Continental Shelf and opening oil shale on federal land.
The Interior Secretary must waive any federal law requiring a drilling permit whenever the West Texas Intermediate crude price is at or above $100 per barrel, and may waive it at lower prices.

The Department of Energy would coordinate all federal and state refinery approvals on a schedule it sets, and would be required to award approval itself within 30 days of any agency missing a deadline.

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the environmental cost of drilling on protected public lands, offshore waters, and oil shale country, with environmental reviews and permitting safeguards suspended when prices are high. State and federal agencies would lose their authority to hold up refinery projects, and taxpayers would be leasing public resources with the protective rules stripped away. Any price relief at the pump would come only after years of development, if it came at all.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public and protected public lands

drawbacks.text: The bill suspends the permitting and environmental processes that apply to drilling on federal lands and waters whenever oil is at or above $100 a barrel, removing review exactly when industry pressure to drill is strongest.

It lets the Secretary of Energy override federal and state agencies by granting refinery approvals on their behalf after a 30-day missed deadline, cutting states and specialized agencies out of decisions on major industrial projects.

The bill's own findings state that building and permitting one offshore platform takes about seven years and roughly $5 billion, so new drilling would not deliver gasoline price relief in the near term for consumers facing $4 gas.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's promise to voters was lower gas prices, but by its own arithmetic the relief would be years away, since offshore production takes roughly seven years to start after permitting. The costs, by contrast, were immediate and certain: federal leasing bans covering most of the Outer Continental Shelf, oil shale lands, and other protected areas would end, and drilling permits could be waived outright whenever prices were high. The bill traded durable environmental protections and agency review for a distant, uncertain consumer benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and their subcommittees, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Michele Bachmann introduced the bill on July 10, 2008, during the summer's record gas-price spike, with 15 Republican cosponsors.
The House referred it to both the Natural Resources Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee, and it was then sent to the Energy and Mineral Resources and Energy and Air Quality subcommittees.
No further action was ever taken; the bill died in committee when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the offshore drilling moratoria, oil shale restrictions, and federal drilling permit requirements all remained in place, so the oil and gas industry gained no new access to protected federal lands and waters. Communities and users of those public lands and waters were spared the suspension of environmental review the bill would have required whenever oil prices were high.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal lands stayed protected; drillers gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Michele Bachmann
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 15 Republican cosponsors.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral that never took up the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die in committee at the end of the Congress.

against.name: 110th Congress House majority
against.role: Democratic majority controlling the House floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were Republicans and the bill never advanced in the Democratic-controlled House committees, so the fight followed party lines, though no vote was ever taken.

industries.note: The bill would hand companies access to protected federal lands, offshore waters, and oil shale, and would waive drilling permits whenever oil topped $100 a barrel. The promised consumer benefit at the pump was uncertain and years away, while the environmental costs of removing review would fall on the public.

The bill would centralize refinery permitting under the Energy Department and force approvals within 30 days of any agency missing a deadline. More refining capacity could modestly help consumers, but it comes by sidelining state and federal agency review.
